name: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
title: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
answer: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers methods that treat risk as more than the standard deviation of returns. It includes downside risk measures such as semi-variance and value at risk, tail measures such as expected shortfall and conditional value at risk, and objectives that account for skewness, kurtosis, drawdown, or the probability of failing a liability or spending goal. It also covers robust and Bayesian formulations that acknowledge estimation error in expected returns and covariances. The scope is not a single model but a family of choices about what to optimise and what to constrain.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on price and return histories, factor exposures, holdings and transaction data, and often on scenario or simulation engines. A site tracking 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices can supply a narrow universe for testing, though most portfolios draw on broader multi-asset data. Computation typically uses numerical optimisation libraries in Python or R, sometimes with GPU acceleration for large scenario sets or resampling. Data quality checks, corporate action adjustments, and time alignment are part of the infrastructure, not an afterthought.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by choosing a risk definition that matches the mandate, then estimate inputs and solve a constrained optimisation problem. Common approaches include mean-CVaR, mean-expected shortfall, downside beta, drawdown-constrained portfolios, and higher-moment or utility-based objectives. Robust methods shrink or penalise uncertain inputs, while resampling and simulation test how sensitive the solution is to small data changes. Backtests and walk-forward tests are used to compare alternatives, with attention to turnover, capacity, and the difference between in-sample fit and out-of-sample behaviour.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The governance section covers data rights, model risk, and the provenance of inputs and code. Price and fundamental data carry licensing terms, and derived signals may inherit restrictions from the underlying sources. Model risk management asks who approved the risk measure, how the optimiser is validated, and how limits and exceptions are documented. Provenance means keeping a clear record of data vintages, transformations, parameter choices, and software versions so that a result can be reproduced or challenged. Where the site tracks 223 compliance and regulation pages, those materials can inform the control environment, but they do not replace jurisdiction-specific review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more explicit tail and drawdown control, more use of scenario and stress testing, and tighter integration with factor and climate or sustainability constraints. Machine learning is being used for return prediction and covariance estimation, but the optimisation layer still needs interpretable risk measures and stable constraints. Practitioners are also paying more attention to implementation shortfall, liquidity, and the cost of rebalancing when risk models become more complex. The likely path is not a single replacement for mean-variance but a menu of risk-aware methods chosen to fit the mandate and the data available.
